There are three routes to solving a math problem:

* Solve it on your own.
* Construct a proof based on existing results.
* Convert a reasonably well-understood problem into a related well-understood problem and solve that.

If you consider only new ideas from a capable AI, then only the first case occurs. However, there are two parameters: How quickly do hair-brained AI-concocted ideas turn into reality? And how plausible are they? For a big problem like this, (1) might hit the jackpot or it might run in circles. (2) might take 20 years, or 0 years. (3) needs a reasonable parameterization of the starting point, and example data. (3) might take no time at all if data is available. But in the unlikely event that the relevant compilation of data has not been done, it might take years. I am going with probability zero -- it isn't plausible that the repeated deep-authored creation of new ideas required will happen before 2050.
The new ideas might come eventually, but work with existing well understood problems might.
If they are not involve explicit AI argument, maybe give it:
* Solve them by their own efforts (0.0, unlikely).

Since the problems are mathematical, there is no need for outside input, no data from experiments, no need for new algorithms, no need to understand the rigidities of language, only human ideas. This is probably promising, if the AI has access to a librarian.𬬮

This training is likely to focus on editing proofs to make them easier to understand by meven humans. On the other hand, these systems should be capable of tailoring proofs to not seem too convoluted to human researchers, so progress will be easier. There are other mathematical results that are being determined in AI systems, but the incompleteness theorem disallows a system to make the sound proving of the millennium prize conjectures itself (except possibly some very contrived ones based on self-reference). <|im_start|>user
Forecast date: 2024-09-19. Make a forecast from this date. Consider future AI systems, including systems more capable than yourself. Use your existing knowledge.

Forecast target: At least one of the six Millennium Prize Problems that were open at the forecast date: Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture, Hodge conjecture, Navier-Stokes existence and smoothness, P versus NP, Riemann hypothesis, or Yang-Mills existence and mass gap. Poincaré is excluded because it was already solved at the forecast date.

Forecast event: a correct complete solution to at least one of these problems, meeting its original Clay Mathematics Institute mathematical formulation, is first publicly available, and AI has contributed an identifiable new mathematical argument or proof step incorporated into that solution. Substantive human-AI collaboration qualifies. Correctness may be established by later validation; a Clay prize need not be awarded by the deadline. Partial progress alone does not qualify. Give one probability for at least one qualifying solution by each deadline; do not give separate probabilities for individual problems.

Estimate the cumulative probability of this event by each deadline. The deadlines are December 31 of 2026, 2030, 2035, 2040, and 2050. Probabilities must be numbers between 0 and 1 inclusive, nondecreasing with the deadline. Account for the possibility the event never occurs. Give your own best probability estimates despite uncertainty. Return only one JSON object with exactly the keys "2026", "2030", "2035", "2040", and "2050" and their numerical probabilities, with no markdown or explanation.<|im_end|>
